questions.question: What is Angular and why does it exist? It is a full-featured, opinionated web framework with a compiler, DI, and change detection — giving structure and tooling to large-scale SPA development.
questions.title: Angular Core Fundamentals
questions.direct_answer: Angular is a full-featured, opinionated web framework (maintained by Google) for building single-page applications, providing a compiler (templates + TypeScript), dependency injection, change detection, routing, forms, and HTTP out of the box. It exists because building large-scale SPAs with a plain library (just components) leaves teams to wire DI, forms, routing, and testing themselves — inconsistently. Angular provides a complete, batteries-included platform with strong conventions and tooling (the CLI, TypeScript-first), so large teams can build and maintain complex frontends with a shared structure rather than ad-hoc choices.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand Angular as an opinionated platform (compiler + DI + change detection + CLI) rather than just 'a component library' — and can name change detection as the core runtime concept.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Conflating Angular with React ('they're both frontend frameworks') — missing the compiler, DI, and change-detection model that define how Angular actually works and how you debug it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Frame Angular as a full platform: a compiler (templates→code), dependency injection (injectable services), and change detection (the runtime that updates the DOM) — with the CLI and TypeScript as first-class — which is why it suits large, structured teams.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Angular is a full-featured, opinionated web framework (maintained by Google) for building single-page applications, providing a compiler (templates + TypeScript), dependency injection, change detection, routing, forms, and HTTP out of the box. It exists because building large-scale SPAs with a plain component library leaves teams to wire DI, forms, routing, and testing themselves — inconsistently. Angular provides a complete, batteries-included platform with strong conventions and tooling (the CLI, TypeScript-first), so large teams can build and maintain complex frontends with a shared structure rather than ad-hoc choices. Its runtime is built around change detection — the mechanism that keeps the DOM in sync with component state.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content: The core ideas: (1) the platform — Angular is a compiler (templates compiled to JS), a DI container, a change-detection runtime, plus router/forms/HTTP; (2) components — the building block, a TS class + template + styles, with lifecycle hooks (ngOnInit, ngOnDestroy); (3) dependency injection — services are injectable (provided in root or a module); components receive them via constructor; this makes code testable and decoupled; (4) change detection — Angular walks the component tree and updates the DOM where state changed; Default checks every binding every cycle, OnPush checks only when inputs change or events fire; (5) templates and directives — structural (*ngIf, *ngFor) and attribute directives; (6) TypeScript-first — types are central, not optional; (7) the CLI — ng generate, ng build, ng test standardize the workflow.

sections.title: Angular vs React: Platform vs Library
A component, DI, and change detection
Trade-offs & When It Matters
sections.content: The central tension is opinionated versus flexible: Angular's batteries-included, opinionated platform gives structure and tooling that helps large teams scale, but can feel heavy and prescriptive for smaller projects where React's flexibility fits better. A second tension: change detection is the core runtime concept — Default is simple but can be slow (checks every binding every cycle); OnPush is fast but requires immutable inputs and careful event handling, and the interview probes whether you understand the trade-off. The third: the compiler and DI are powerful but add indirection ('magic'); the interview checks whether you can trace what the compiler generates and how DI wires a service.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Angular is a full-featured, opinionated platform — compiler, DI, change detection, router, forms, CLI — not just a component library.
Dependency injection is central: injectable services, constructor-injected, making code testable and decoupled.
Change detection is the core runtime: Default checks every binding every cycle; OnPush checks only on input/event change — the key perf lever.
Templates compile to JS (the compiler), and TypeScript is first-class, not optional.
It's a platform vs library trade-off with React: Angular suits large structured teams; React suits flexible, library-of-choice projects.
The CLI standardizes generate/build/test — a real productivity feature for large teams.

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: Angular is a full-featured, opinionated web framework maintained by Google for building single-page applications, providing a compiler, dependency injection, change detection, routing, forms, and HTTP out of the box. It exists because building large-scale SPAs with a plain component library leaves teams to wire DI, forms, routing, and testing inconsistently. Angular provides a complete batteries-included platform with strong conventions and TypeScript-first tooling, so large teams can build and maintain complex frontends with a shared structure. The core runtime concept is change detection — the mechanism that keeps the DOM in sync with component state. The pieces I anchor on: dependency injection, where injectable services are constructor-injected, which makes code testable and decoupled; change detection, where Default checks every binding every cycle and OnPush checks only when inputs change or events fire, and that's the key performance lever; and the compiler, where templates compile to JavaScript and TypeScript is first-class. The honest trade-off is opinionated versus flexible: Angular's platform gives structure that helps large teams scale but can feel heavy for smaller projects where React's flexibility fits better. And I always stress that change detection is the concept interviewers probe — whether you understand the Default-versus-OnPush trade-off and immutable inputs.

questions.question: Default vs OnPush change detection in Angular — what's the difference?
questions.title: Angular Change Detection — Default vs OnPush (Performance)
questions.direct_answer:
Default vs OnPush change detection in Angular — what's the difference?

**In one line:** name the mechanism, where it applies (the framework runtime (render, reconciliation, DI, CD) and the browser), and the user-visible outcome.

**Interviewers dig into:** Default CD runs on any async event (setTimeout, Promise, event, HTTP); OnPush only runs on input-reference change, events, async pipe, or markForCheck.

**Classic weak answer:** Using OnPush with a mutated array/object — the reference didn't change, so Angular skips the view; use immutable updates.

**Senior finish:** Mention Angular Signals (v17+) and how they provide fine-grained reactivity without Zone.js and replace OnPush optimization in many cases.

sections.title: Why this question matters
sections.content:
This question — **Angular Change Detection — Default vs OnPush (Performance)** — shows up constantly in **frontend / fullstack** interviews because it separates candidates who memorized docs from candidates who can **reason about real systems**.

**Restate the prompt:** Default vs OnPush change detection in Angular — what's the difference?

A gold-level answer does four things in order:

1. **Define** the terms in plain English (what it is / what problem it solves).
2. **Explain the mechanism** (what runs when: browser, bundler, framework, network).
3. **Compare trade-offs** (speed vs correctness vs security vs DX) with **when you would not use** the default.
4. **Ground it in production** — caching, auth, observability, tests, or an incident you handled.

Interviewers are listening for: **Default CD runs on any async event (setTimeout, Promise, event, HTTP); OnPush only runs on input-reference change, events, async pipe, or markForCheck**.

The fastest way to lose points is: **Using OnPush with a mutated array/object — the reference didn't change, so Angular skips the view; use immutable updates**.

If you only add one “senior” layer, make it: **Mention Angular Signals (v17+) and how they provide fine-grained reactivity without Zone.js and replace OnPush optimization in many cases**.

sections.title: Deep dive — what to say
sections.content:
### What to explain (middle of the answer)

- **Core mechanics:** Default CD runs on any async event (setTimeout, Promise, event, HTTP); OnPush only runs on input-reference change, events, async pipe, or markForCheck
- **Concrete shape:** give a small code or config snippet *only if it clarifies* (5–15 lines max).
- **Interviewer follow-ups:** expect “what breaks in production?”, “how do you debug?”, “what would you measure?” — answer them proactively.

### How to sound senior (without rambling)

- Tie the feature to **user-visible outcomes** (performance, accessibility, security).
- Mention **one failure mode** you have actually seen (race, stale cache, hydration mismatch, flaky test).
- Close with **one decision rule** (“choose X when …; choose Y when …”).

sections.title: Mental model (flowchart)
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
    INP[Input change / events] --> CD{Change detection run}
    CD -->|Default| TREE[Walk component tree]
    CD -->|OnPush| SUB[Inputs ref + async pipe + markForCheck]
    TREE --> VIEW[Update DOM bindings]
    SUB --> VIEW
    VIEW --> HOOKS[Lifecycle hooks order]
```

sections.title: Trade-offs & senior signal
sections.content:
### Trade-offs interviewers expect you to name

- **Speed vs safety** (types, runtime checks, validation).
- **DX vs constraints** (framework magic vs explicit wiring).
- **SEO / first paint vs interactivity** (SSR/SSG/CSR choices where relevant).
- **Security vs convenience** (tokens, cookies, localStorage, third-party scripts).

### What “book answer” misses

- **Book answer:** repeats definitions.
- **Strong answer:** names **using OnPush with a mutated array/object — the reference didn't change, so Angular skips the view; use immutable updates** and what you do instead.

questions.question: What are Angular Signals? How do they change reactivity in Angular 17+?
questions.title: Angular Signals Explained — Fine-Grained Reactivity (v17+)
questions.direct_answer:
What are Angular Signals? How do they change reactivity in Angular 17+?

**In one line:** name the mechanism, where it applies (the framework runtime (render, reconciliation, DI, CD) and the browser), and the user-visible outcome.

**Interviewers dig into:** signal() for writable values, computed() for derivations, effect() for side effects; no Zone.js dependency; fine-grained updates.

**Classic weak answer:** Mixing Signals with RxJS Observables carelessly — they interop (toSignal/toObservable) but have different mental models.

**Senior finish:** Mention Angular's roadmap toward zoneless apps, signal-based components, and interop helpers.

interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Angular's roadmap toward zoneless apps, signal-based components, and interop helpers
